11diqwu: This week you review two classes that help you talk about changes in your life. The first helps you say how an action ends: whether it has just happened, whether you complete it, whether you abandon it or how far it goes. The second helps you talk about what is repeated or what you take up again after a break. Your guide is Nuria, a teacher from Granada who has just finished a challenge: thirty days without social media.
16rm8bl: “Acabar de”: a moment ago or already finished
qv90vw: In the present, “acabar de + infinitive” places an action in the very recent past: “Acabo de apagar el móvil” (a minute ago). In a story in the past, the imperfect does the same: “Acababa de salir de clase cuando me llamó mi hermana”.
11sx1mf: In the preterite, the present perfect or the future, however, “acabar de” means the same as “terminar de”: completing something that was already under way. “Ayer acabé de leer la novela” means I read the last pages, not that I read it a moment ago.
3b3yz3: To say that something happened a moment ago, use the present “acabo de”.
1xoklq7: “Acabo de” is a recent past: it does not combine with a distant time like “hace dos años”.
1f32yxq: Terminar de, dejar de, llegar a and acabar + gerund
oxwwos: “Terminar de” completes a task: “Termino de fregar y salgo”. “Dejar de” interrupts or abandons an activity or a habit, even if it is not finished: “Dejé de mirar el móvil en la cama”. With “no” in front, “no dejar de” means to keep on without stopping (“No deja de llover”), and in the imperative it is a friendly invitation: “No dejes de visitar el Albaicín”.
1b9o1f4: For the end of a story you have two more tools. “Llegar a + infinitive” marks the highest point, sometimes a surprising one: “Llegué a pasar seis horas al día con el móvil”. “Acabar + gerund” (or “acabar por + infinitive”) tells the final result after a process: “Al final acabé apagándolo todo”.
160lqhe: Ask yourself: was the action completed (terminar de) or cut off before it finished (dejar de)?

149rjbi: To recommend something you use the negative imperative: “no dejes de”.
m6mdcj: “Volver a + infinitive”: again, in any tense
f6spqo: “Volver a + infinitive” means “again”: an action is repeated or taken up again after a break. Only “volver” is conjugated; the infinitive does not change: “vuelvo a leer”, “volví a leer”, “he vuelto a leer”, “volveré a leer”, “espero que vuelvas a leer”.
1e84ghf: Pronouns go before “volver” or attached to the infinitive, never in both places: “Lo volví a instalar” or “Volví a instalarlo”. With pronominal verbs the same thing happens: “Se volvió a caer la red” or “Volvió a caerse la red”.
1tro4zv: Volver a in the tenses you already know
1lafqp6: The pronoun goes in only one place: before “volver” or after the infinitive.
z4h9ct: After “volver a” the verb is always in the infinitive.
1b6zh60: No volver a, otra vez, repetir and the prefix re-
ac69s1: In the negative, “no volver a” means “never again”: you use it to promise (“No volverá a pasar”), to warn (“No vuelvas a contestar ese correo”) or to say that something did not happen again (“Nunca volví a verla”). Don’t confuse it with “dejar de”: “dejé de ir al gimnasio” says that a habit ended; “no volví a ir al gimnasio” says that, after one time, I never went again.
1p1vea8: To repeat you also have “otra vez” and “de nuevo” (“Lo leí otra vez”), “repetir” + noun (“Repetí el examen”; never “repetí a hacer”) and the prefix “re-” in some verbs (releer, rehacer, reenviar). Careful: “volver a + a place” means to return: “Volví a Granada en 2020”.
vfvyir: If you can add “otra vez” at the end of the sentence without changing the meaning, “volver a” is the natural choice.

uya20s: Acabo / acabó, dejo / dejó: the stressed syllable changes the tense
sqfnm7: In this week’s verbs, a single strong syllable separates the present from the past. “Acabo de” (a-CA-bo) talks about you right now; “acabó de” (a-ca-BÓ) says that someone else finished something. The same happens with “dejo / dejó” and “termino / terminó”. If you change the stress, you change the tense and the person.
1gazps1: With “volver” the difference is also in the vowel: “vuelvo” and “vuelve” have “ue” in the strong syllable, but “volví” and “volvió” have “o” because the stress moves to the end. Also, “a” joins the next vowel without a pause: “vuelvo‿a‿hacerlo”, “acaba‿de‿empezar”.
7ambj0: The written accent marks the difference in writing: “acabo / acabó”, “dejo / dejó”, “termino / terminó”. If you forget it in a message, you change the tense and the person of the verb.

1l7iqzx: Day 31: what I gave up and what I got back
1lu3w4u: Nuria writes a blog about life in Granada. This is the post she published the day after finishing her challenge.
1cm9bd1: Today is day 31 and I’ve just opened my laptop to write this, not to look at social media. A month ago I decided to do an experiment: thirty days without Instagram or TikTok. My screen time had reached five hours a day, and the worst thing wasn’t the hours, but the feeling of never finishing anything.
a0314f: The first thing I stopped doing was looking at my phone as soon as I woke up. The first few days I picked it up anyway, out of sheer habit, and stared at a screen with nothing to see. I had a relapse on day twelve: I installed an app again “just for a moment” and ended up spending a whole hour swiping. That night I deleted it again and never fell back into it.
16hrex5: What I’ve got back has surprised me. I’ve started reading before bed again, I’ve started phoning my friends again instead of sending them a heart, and on Sunday I walked up to the Sacromonte again, something I hadn’t done since university. I also finished sorting the photos from my trip to Morocco, which had been waiting for two years.
vy3pb2: And now? I don’t intend to go back to my old life. I’ll keep just one social network and look at it in the afternoon. If you’re thinking of doing something similar, be sure to try: the first week is hard, but it’s worth it.
